'''Ruth Hege Howes''' (October 18, 1944 – April 29, 2025)<ref>{{Cite web |title=DNB, Katalog der Deutschen Nationalbibliothek |url=https://portal.dnb.de/opac.htm?method=simpleSearch&cqlMode=true&query=nid%3D14142169X |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=portal.dnb.de}}</ref> was an American [[Nuclear physics|nuclear physicist]], expert on nuclear weapons, and [[History of science|historian of science]], known for her books on [[women in physics]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Ruth Howes - Nuclear Museum |url=https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/profile/ruth-howes/ |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=Nuclear Museum}}</ref> Throughout her career, she also contributed greatly to advancing undergraduate physics education.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ruth Howes {{!}} American Institute of Physics |url=https://www.aip.org/ruth-howes |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=www.aip.org}}</ref> As co-author of several books that put a spotlight on the careers of female scientists, including those involved in the Manhattan Project, she considerably increased female scientists' recognition. 

==Early life and education==
Ruth Hege was born October 18, 1944 in [[Montpelier, Vermont|Montpelier]], [[Vermont]], to James Landes and Marvin (Colton) Hege.<ref name=":1">"Ruth Hege Howes." ''American Men & Women of Science'': ''A Biographical Directory of Today's Leaders in Physical, Biological, and Related Sciences'', Gale, 2008. ''Gale In Context: Biography'', link.gale.com/apps/doc/K3099053009/BIC?u=columbiau&sid=summon&xid=9aefb4ae. Accessed 15 Mar. 2025.</ref> In 1962, she graduated from [[Northfield Mount Hermon School|Northfield Mount Hermon]] boarding school in [[Gill, Massachusetts|Gill]], [[Massachusetts]].<ref>Ruth Howes. ''About'' [Facebook Page]. Facebook. Retrieved March 15, 2025, from https://www.facebook.com/ruth.howes.37/about_work_and_education</ref> She earned her bachelor's degree from [[Mount Holyoke College]] in 1965,<ref name=":1" /> later revealing that she "studied physics in college because it was the most beautiful intellectual endeavor [she] ever encountered."<ref name="MjtTb">{{cite journal | last1=Howes | first1=Ruth | title=Modern physics — Guest editorial | journal=The Physics Teacher | date=2000 | volume=38 | issue=2 | page=73 | doi=10.1119/1.880457 | bibcode=2000PhTea..38...73H }}</ref> After college, she earned her MA from [[Columbia University]] in 1967 and her PhD in physics from Columbia University in 1971.<ref name=":1" /> Hege conducted her doctoral research under physicist [[Chien-Shiung Wu]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Speakers & Panelists {{!}} CUWiP @ UTSA & SwRI |url=https://www.utsa.edu/physics/cuwip2016/conference/speakers.html |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=www.utsa.edu}}</ref> focusing largely on the [[Mössbauer effect|Mossbauer Effect]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chow |first1=Y. W. |last2=Howes |first2=R. H. |last3=Swerdlow |first3=P. H. |last4=Yen |first4=C. S. |last5=Wu |first5=C. S. |date=1970-01-01 |title= Mössbauer measurements of quadrupole-moment ratios of the first excited 2<sup>+</sup> states of <sup>176, 178 and 180</sup>Hf|url=https://www.osti.gov/biblio/4095655 |journal= Physics Letters B|volume=32 |issue=8 |pages=682–684 |language=English |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(70)90444-2|bibcode=1970PhLB...32..682C |osti=4095655 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chow |first1=Y. W. |last2=Greenbaum |first2=E. S. |last3=Howes |first3=R. H. |last4=Hsu |first4=F. H. H. |last5=Swerdlow |first5=P. H. |last6=Wu |first6=C. S. |date=1969-01-01 |title= Mössbauer effect following coulomb excitation measurements of electric quadrupole moment ratios in the first excited 2<sup>+</sup> states of <sup>182,4,6</sup>W|url=https://www.osti.gov/biblio/4739465 |journal= Physics Letters B|volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=171–174 |language=English |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(69)90361-X|bibcode=1969PhLB...30..171C |osti=4739465 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chow |first1=Y. W. |last2=Greenbaum |first2=E. S. |last3=Howes |first3=R. H. |last4=Hsu |first4=F. H. H. |last5=Swerdlow |first5=P. H. |last6=Wu |first6=C. S. |date=1968-01-01 |title=The use of a helium refrigerator for Mössbauer studies |url=https://www.osti.gov/biblio/4806833 |journal= Nuclear Instruments and Methods|volume=66 |issue=1 |pages=177–180 |language=English |doi=10.1016/0029-554X(68)90078-5|bibcode=1968NucIM..66..177C |osti=4806833 }}</ref> In 1971, her thesis, "Measurements of Quadrupole-Moment Ratios of the First Excited 2<sup>+</sup> states of <sup>176, 178, and 180</sup>Hf using the Mössbauer Effect Following Coulomb Excitation," was published.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Howes |first=Ruth |title=Measurements of quadrupole-moment ratios of the first excited 2<sup>+</sup> states of <sup>176, 178, and 180</sup>Hf using the Mössbauer effect following Coulomb excitation |publisher=Columbia |year=1971 |location=New York |publication-date=1971}}</ref>

==Research and career==
Howes began her career in academia as a visiting assistant physics professor at the [[University of Oklahoma]] from 1971 to 1972.<ref name=":1" /> She then served as an adjunct instructor at [[Oklahoma City University]] from 1972 to 1976.<ref name=":1" /> In 1976, she joined the faculty at [[Ball State University]], becoming the university’s first female physics professor.<ref name=":2">{{cite journal | last1=Watson | first1=Jim | title=Meet your new President: Ruth Howes | journal=The Physics Teacher | date=2000 | volume=38 | issue=2 | page=72 | doi=10.1119/1.880456 | bibcode=2000PhTea..38...72W }}</ref> She was later named the George and Frances Ball Distinguished Professor of Physics and Astronomy in 1991.<ref name=":1" />

Howes was an advocate of the importance of science in directing national security policy. In 1984, on a sabbatical from Ball State University, she was selected as a William C. Foster Fellow at the [[Arms Control and Disarmament Agency|US Arms Control and Disarmament Agency]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3">{{cite book | last1=Howes | first1=Ruth H. | last2=Herzenberg | first2=Caroline L. | title=After the War: Women in Physics in the United States | date=2015 | doi=10.1088/978-1-6817-4094-2 | bibcode=2015awwp.book.....H | isbn=978-1-6817-4094-2 }}</ref><ref name=":4">{{cite journal | last1=Chiaverina | first1=Chris | title=2004 Distinguished Service Citations Awarded: Ruth Howes | journal=The Physics Teacher | date=2004 | volume=42 | issue=4 | pages=200–201 | doi=10.1119/1.1696582 | bibcode=2004PhTea..42..200C }}</ref> From 1987 to 1992, Howes served as director of the Center for Global Security Studies at Ball State University.<ref name=":2" /> She published a guest editorial on nuclear physics in the ''International Journal on World Peace'' in 1988, in which she discussed how nations can realistically reduce the threat of [[nuclear warfare]].<ref>Howes, R. (1988). COMMENT. ''International Journal on World Peace, 5''(4), 59. Retrieved from https://www.proquest.com/docview/1311351516 </ref> Howes was elected as a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1992 for the influential role that her [[ballistic missile]] research played in the negotiations for [[START I]], a crucial disarmament agreement between the U.S. and [[Soviet Union]] signed in 1991.<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Fellows Archive |url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/aps-fellowship |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=www.aps.org |language=en}}</ref> Her later research, specifically an article she co-authored on the "Technical Debate Over Patriot Performance In the Gulf War," also influenced national security policy. Her research demonstrated that video analysis suggested that the Patriot PAC-2 theater missile had a success rate close to 0% in the war, despite claims by the U.S. Army that the Patriot PAC-2 theater missile had a 61% success rate in the war and a 100% success rate in testing. On May 4, 1999, Dr. David C. Wright cited her research before the U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations Hearing "Ballistic Missiles: Threat and Response." Using her work as evidence that weapons may seem successful in testing and fail in reality, Wright argued that the United States was not ready to deploy ballistic missile weapons, significantly aiding U.S. and Russian disarmament.<ref>{{Cite web |title=S.Hrg. 106-339 — BALLISTIC MISSILES: THREAT AND RESPONSE |url=https://www.congress.gov/event/106th-congress/senate-event/LC66586/text |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=www.congress.gov}}</ref> 

Throughout her career, Howes was devoted to advancing science education. Drawn to Ball State by the opportunity to develop a "Colloquium in Science and Math" course for non-science majors, Howes was determined to improve science education for all students. While teaching this course, she earned the nickname, "Madame Ruth, [[Psychic]] to the Stars," at Ball State University.<ref name=":2" /> 

Howes published several articles on improving physics education in several notable journals, including the ''[[American Journal of Physics]]'', ''[[The Physics Teacher]]'', ''[[Physics Today]]'', and the ''Journal of College Science Teachers''.<ref name=":5">{{cite journal | last1=Howes | first1=Ruth | last2=Watson | first2=James | title=Science and Pseudoscience: A Course for the Citizen of the Twenty-First Century | journal=Journal of College Science Teaching | date=1981 | volume=11 | issue=2 | pages=105–107 | jstor=42988368 | url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/42988368 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Howes | first1=Ruth | last2=Watson | first2=James | title=Demonstrations to wake up large classes | journal=The Physics Teacher | date=1982 | volume=20 | issue=1 | pages=40–41 | doi=10.1119/1.2340932 | bibcode=1982PhTea..20...40H }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Howes | first1=Ruth H. | last2=Lyons | first2=K. B. | title=Guest Comment: Why the APS must concern itself with education | journal=American Journal of Physics | date=1994 | volume=62 | issue=5 | pages=395–396 | doi=10.1119/1.17538 | bibcode=1994AmJPh..62..395H }}</ref><ref name=":6">{{cite journal | last1=Howes | first1=Ruth H. | last2=Hilborn | first2=Robert C. | title=Winds of Change | journal=American Journal of Physics | date=2000 | volume=68 | issue=5 | pages=401–402 | doi=10.1119/1.19468 | bibcode=2000AmJPh..68..401H }}</ref><ref name="MjtTb" /><ref name=":7">{{cite journal | last1=Hilborn | first1=Robert C. | last2=Howes | first2=Ruth H. | title=Why Many Undergraduate Physics Programs Are Good but Few Are Great | journal=Physics Today | date=2003 | volume=56 | issue=9 | pages=38–44 | doi=10.1063/1.1620833 | bibcode=2003PhT....56i..38H }}</ref> Howes also served as an [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] Congressional Fellow from 1993 to 1994,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Historic Fellows {{!}} American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) |url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/historic |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=www.aaas.org |language=en}}</ref> working in the education office of the Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources on improving general science policy and higher education funding.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Cioffi | first1=Denis F. | title=Congressional Fellows Add Their Expertise to the Political Process | journal=Physics Today | date=1995 | volume=48 | issue=3 | pages=84–85 | doi=10.1063/1.2807943 | bibcode=1995PhT....48c..84C }}</ref> From 1994 to 1995, Howes served as program director for undergraduate physics programs at the [[National Science Foundation]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=2003-04-25 |title=Ball State University Alpha and Omega Recognition Ceremony program |url=https://cardinalscholar.bsu.edu/items/d88ff9cb-51c5-433a-a2e6-83ab7d400898 |language=en}}</ref> and as chair of the [[American Physical Society]] Forum on Education in 1996.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Council Approves Mass Media Fellowship Program |url=https://www.aps.org/archives/publications/apsnews/199602/fellowship-program.cfm |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=www.aps.org |language=en}}</ref> She was a leader of the [[American Association of Physics Teachers]], serving as president from 2000 to 2001,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Presidents of AAPT |url=https://aapt.org/aboutaapt/history/presidents.cfm |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=aapt.org}}</ref> deputy chair of the National Task Force on Undergraduate Physics, and principal author of a module for the Active Physics Writing Team.<ref name=":4" /> She also helped develop the AAPT Strategic Programs for Innovations in Undergraduate Education (SPIN-UP) program.<ref name=":4" />

In the early 1990s, Howes began editing books, beginning with ''The Energy Sourcebook'' (American Institute of Physics, 1991), co-edited with Anthony Fainberg.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/energysourcebook0000unse/mode/2up |title=The Energy sourcebook : a guide to technology, resources, and policy |date=1991 |publisher=New York : American Institute of Physics |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-88318-706-7}}</ref> While working on ''Women and the Use of Military Force'' (Lynne Rienner Publishers, 1993),<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Howes |first1=Ruth |title=Women and the Use of Military Force |last2=Stevenson |first2=Michael |publisher=Lynne Rienner Publishers |year=1993 |isbn=1-55587-329-4 |location=United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland |publication-date=1993}}</ref> Howes and co-editor [[Caroline Herzenberg]] were asked to write a chapter on the role of female physicists involved in the [[Manhattan Project]].<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=Hafner |first=Katie |title=They Remembered the Lost Women of the Manhattan Project So That None of Us Would Forget |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/they-remembered-the-lost-women-of-the-manhattan-project-so-that-none-of-us-would-forget/ |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref> Most accounts had excluded the role of women in the project, and several of Howes and Herzenberg's colleagues laughed at how short their chapter would be, believing that very few women were involved. However, Howes and Herzenberg were put into contact with [[Naomi Livesay]], who had worked at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]] and gave them information on other female scientists who were instrumental in the project. As Howes and Herzenberg began following French's leads, they rapidly discovered a network of over 300 women who had been involved with the Manhattan Project.<ref name=":9" /> Howes and Herzenberg published an article in ''Physics Today'' on the role of female physicists at Los Alamos<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Howes | first1=Ruth H. | last2=Herzenberg | first2=Caroline L. | title=Calculating Women Had Major Wartime Roles at los Alamos | journal=Physics Today | date=1997 | volume=50 | issue=3 | pages=105–106 | doi=10.1063/1.881686 | bibcode=1997PhT....50c.105H }}</ref> and later co-authored the book, ''Their Day in the Sun: Women of the Manhattan Project'' (Temple University Press, 1999).<ref name=":10">Howes, R. & Herzenberg, C. L. (1999) ''Their Day in the Sun: Women of the Manhattan Project''. Philadelphia, PA: Temple University Press. [Web.] Retrieved from the Library of Congress, https://lccn.loc.gov/99017683.</ref> In 2015, the pair published ''After the War: Women in Physics in the United States'' (Morgan Claypool Press, 2015), which documented the careers of female physicists in the post war era.<ref name=":9" />

== Personal life ==
Ruth Hege married physicist Robert I. Howes Jr. on June 4, 1966.<ref name=":1" /> Robert Howes' father, Robert I. Howes Sr., was involved in the [[Manhattan Project]] at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]] as an [[Electrical engineering|electrical engineer]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Robert Howes Sr. - Nuclear Museum |url=https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/profile/robert-howes-sr/ |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=Nuclear Museum |language=en-US}}</ref>

Ruth and Bob Howes had two children, Rachel T. and Prudence N. Howes.<ref name=":1" /> After retiring from her position at Marquette University in 2008, Howes moved to [[Santa Fe, New Mexico]].<ref name=":3" /> She died in Santa Fe on April 29, 2025, at the age of 80.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/santafenewmexican/name/ruth-howes-obituary?id=61070859|title=Ruth Hege Howes|work=Santa Fe New Mexican|date=March 21, 2026}}</ref>
